haegeum 為韓國傳統弦鳴樂器，源於古代中國奚琴；中文資料記唐朝末期傳入中國: The haegeum is a traditional Korean chordophone, descended from the ancient Chinese xiqin; Chinese sources record that it came to China at the end of the Tang dynasty and later spread to the Korean peninsula and Japan. The exact date it reached Korea is unrecorded; the Goryeo-period hanlimbyeolgok mentions it, so it can be assumed to have been played at least from that period. In the Joseon dynasty it was used for royal sacrifices, processions, festivals and hyangak. In the mid-Joseon the playing method changed from the gyeongan method to the yeogan method, and because there is no fingerboard the string can be pressed and released for a variety of sounds. From the 1960s it was improved: in 1965 Park Hun-bong and Kim Bun-gi made a low-pitched haegeum, and in 1967 Kim Gisu made a small haegeum; North Korea separately developed a four-string small haegeum.
奚琴的琴身以木製空心音箱與棍狀琴頸為主，發聲體為兩條絲弦，演奏時使用木弓擦弦。另: The haegeum's body is a hollow wooden soundbox with a stick-shaped neck, and the sound comes from two silk strings, bowed with a wooden bow. Other sources say the traditional haegeum was made of the eight materials metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, earth, hide and wood, hence the name "eight sounds", but they do not say which part corresponds to which material. The improved small haegeum of North Korea has four silk strings, with the pegs turned the opposite way from the erhu and metal screw tuning machines at the head; the materials of the remaining parts are not stated.

弓毛拉出的哭與唱（擦弦、輪弦與提琴家族）: Weeping and singing drawn from bow hair (bowed strings, wheel-bowed strings and the violin family)
演奏時將琴身垂直置於膝上，身體略向前彎，以木弓置於兩條絲弦之間摩擦發聲。其發聲屬: To play, hold the instrument upright on the knee, lean the body slightly forward, and put the wooden bow between the two silk strings to set them sounding by friction. The sound is produced as on any chordophone, the bow touching the string and the hollow wooden soundbox resonating. Because there is no fingerboard, a beginner must first steady the bow and the position of the strings, then press and release the silk strings with the fingers to change the sound. Before the mid-Joseon there was a way of pressing the strings without bowing; later the bowed technique developed, which gives a wider variety of sound.
細長鼻音、宮廷與民俗情緒｜弓毛拉出的哭與唱（擦弦、輪弦與提琴家族）: slender nasal tone, court and folk feeling | Weeping and singing drawn from bow hair (bowed strings, wheel-bowed strings and the violin family)
韓國奚琴音色溫潤悠揚，具有獨特的人聲化特質，音質介於小提琴的明亮與二胡的深沉之間: The Korean haegeum's timbre is warm and long-drawn, with a distinctive vocal quality: it lies between the brightness of the violin and the depth of the erhu. Its two silk strings sound penetrating without losing softness; the low register is full and deep, while the middle and top reveal a plaintive, turning emotional tension. The hollow wooden soundbox amplifies the vibration effectively, so the sound wave spreads and rings well. Against the sharp brilliance of the Western violin the haegeum has more Eastern character and a slightly weathered feel; against the vigour of the erhu its tone is warmer. Its range is wide and it can produce fine glissando and vibrato, which is why Korean traditional music uses it for deep national feeling and courtly elegance.
韩国奚琴是韩国传统弓弦乐器，属弦鸣乐器，源自古代中国奚琴。构造有棍状琴颈、空心木: The Korean haegeum is a traditional Korean bowed instrument, a chordophone, descended from the ancient Chinese xiqin. It has a stick-shaped neck, a hollow wooden soundbox and two silk strings; the player leans forward, holds the instrument upright on the knee, and bows with a wooden bow between the two strings. It is widely used in Korean music, in court music, hyangak and folk mannori (folk music), and also for royal sacrifices, processions and festivals. Traditionally it was made of the eight materials metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, earth, hide and wood, hence the name "eight sounds".
